slides.title: Factorising a quadratic
slides.lede: 5 minutes. What factorising asks, and the two forms you will meet today.

keyIdea.title: Key idea
keyIdea.body: Factorising asks the expanding question backwards: which two brackets multiply to give this expression? Every answer can be checked by expanding it again.

concepts.body: Expanding turns (_x_ + 2)(_x_ + 3) into _x_^2 + 5_x_ + 6. Factorising turns it back. If your factors expand to the original, you are right.
A quadratic is monic when the coefficient of _x_^2 is 1 — _x_^2 + _b__x_ + _c_.
A quadratic is non-monic when the coefficient of _x_^2 is not 1 — _a__x_^2 + _b__x_ + _c_ with _a_ ≠ 1.
For a monic quadratic, find two numbers that MULTIPLY to _c_ and ADD to _b_. Those two numbers go straight into the brackets.
Always look for a common factor before anything else. 2_x_^2 + 10_x_ + 12 becomes 2(_x_^2 + 5_x_ + 6), and the bracket is now monic.
If _c_ is positive, both numbers share the sign of _b_. If _c_ is negative, one number is positive and one is negative.

examples.label: Finding the pair
examples.caption: Every factor pair of 12, and what each pair adds to.

parts.body: To factorise _x_^2 + 7_x_ + 12 you need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7. Listing the factor pairs makes the search finite — there are only three to try.

examples.label: What the signs tell you
examples.caption: Read the sign of the constant first, then the sign of the middle term.

items: _x_^2 + 7_x_ + 12 — constant positive, middle positive → both numbers positive: (_x_ + 3)(_x_ + 4).
_x_^2 − 7_x_ + 12 — constant positive, middle negative → both numbers negative: (_x_ − 3)(_x_ − 4).
_x_^2 + _x_ − 12 — constant negative → one of each sign: (_x_ + 4)(_x_ − 3).
_x_^2 − _x_ − 12 — constant negative → one of each sign, the larger taking the middle sign: (_x_ − 4)(_x_ + 3).

slides.title: Factorising monic quadratics
slides.lede: 6 minutes. Play your own video here; this page carries the frame, what to watch for, and what to do after.

video.still: Two numbers that multiply to _c_ and add to _b_.

afterWatching.title: After watching
items: Factorise _x_^2 + 9_x_ + 20 without writing anything down first — say the pair out loud.
Expand your answer to check it. If it does not come back to the original, the pair was wrong, not the method.

slides.title: Monic quadratics — _x_^2 + _b__x_ + _c_
slides.lede: 10 minutes. Four examples, one for each sign pattern you will meet, and one where a common factor comes out first.

groups.title: Multiply to _c_, add to _b_
groups.lede: The same method three times, with the signs changing each time.

steps.text: Check for a common factor. There is none, and the expression is monic.
The constant is positive and the middle term is positive, so look for two positive numbers.
Test the factor pairs of 12: 1 and 12 add to 13, 2 and 6 add to 8, 3 and 4 add to 7.
Write the two brackets using that pair.
The constant is positive, so both numbers share a sign; the middle term is negative, so both are negative.
Find the pair.
Write the brackets.
The constant is negative, so one number is positive and one is negative.
Find the pair. The larger number takes the sign of the middle term.
Write the brackets.
Check by expanding.

groups.title: Take the common factor out first
groups.lede: A quadratic that looks non-monic is often a monic one in disguise.

examples.label: A common factor

steps.text: Every term is divisible by 2. Take it out before anything else.
The bracket is now monic. Find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5.
Factorise the bracket, keeping the 2 in front.

examples.answer: 2_x_^2 + 10_x_ + 12 = 2(_x_ + 2)(_x_ + 3). Leaving the 2 out is the commonest mistake here.

questions.stem: Complete the table for the quadratic _x_^2 + 8_x_ + 15.
Factorise each expression. Both numbers will be negative.
Factorise each expression. The constant is negative, so the signs differ.
Take out the common factor first, then factorise the bracket.
Sasha writes _x_^2 − 4_x_ − 12 = (_x_ − 6)(_x_ − 2). Expand her answer, explain what went wrong, and give the correct factorisation.
parts: Say which sign is wrong and why.

questions.stem: A rectangle has area _x_^2 + 9_x_ + 18 square centimetres. Write expressions for its length and width.
parts: If _x_ = 4, find the actual length, width and area.

slides.title: Factorising non-monic quadratics
slides.lede: 6 minutes. Play your second video here. The method changes: the middle term is split before the brackets appear.

video.still: Multiply _a_ by _c_, split the middle term, then group.

afterWatching.title: After watching
items: For 2_x_^2 + 7_x_ + 3, write down _a_ × _c_ and the pair that adds to _b_ before you factorise anything.
After grouping, the two brackets must be identical. If they are not, the split was wrong — go back one line rather than starting again.

slides.title: Non-monic quadratics — _a__x_^2 + _b__x_ + _c_
slides.lede: 12 minutes. The same four moves every time: multiply, find the pair, split, group.

groups.title: Multiply, split, group
groups.lede: Three examples: both signs positive, both negative, and mixed.

steps.text: There is no common factor, and the leading coefficient is not 1. Multiply the first and last coefficients.
Find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to the middle coefficient, 7.
Split the middle term into those two terms. The order does not matter.
Group in pairs and factorise each pair.
The bracket (2_x_ + 1) is common to both. Take it out.

examples.label: Both signs negative

steps.text: Multiply the first and last coefficients.
The product is positive and the middle term is negative, so both numbers are negative.
Split the middle term.
Group and factorise each pair. Take out −3 from the second pair so the bracket matches.
Take out the common bracket.

examples.answer: 6_x_^2 − 11_x_ + 3 = (3_x_ − 1)(2_x_ − 3). Taking out +3 instead of −3 in step 4 leaves two different brackets — that is the signal to go back one line.

steps.text: Multiply the first and last coefficients. The product is negative, so the two numbers have different signs.
Find the pair that adds to −5.
Split the middle term.
Group and factorise each pair.
Take out the common bracket, then check by expanding.

questions.stem: For each quadratic, write down _a_ × _c_ and the pair of numbers that multiplies to it and adds to _b_. Do not factorise yet.
Factorise each expression. Both numbers in the pair will be negative.
Factorise each expression. The constant is negative, so the pair has mixed signs.
Mixed set — decide first whether there is a common factor, and whether it is monic or non-monic.

parts: Explain how expanding shows it is wrong.

questions.stem: A rectangle has area 2_x_^2 + 7_x_ + 6 square metres and its width is (_x_ + 2) metres.
parts: Write an expression for the length.

concepts.body: Common factor first. Monic: multiply to _c_, add to _b_. Non-monic: multiply _a_ by _c_, split the middle term, group in pairs. Every answer is checked by expanding it.
